subject: Banking
title: Savings and Loan Fraud of the 1980s
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Savings and Loan Fraud of the 1980s.

hook.text: The 1980s S&L crisis cost taxpayers $132 billion. Deregulation let savings banks gamble with depositor money.

buildup.text: Savings and loan banks were designed for home mortgages.

discovery.text: Over 1,000 S&Ls failed. Many were run by fraudsters who used depositor money for luxury lifestyles and bad investments.

twist.text: Charles Keating bribed five US senators to stop regulators from investigating his Lincoln Savings.

climax.text: The S&L crisis proved that deregulation without oversight invites fraud.

quiz.question: What caused the savings and loan crisis?
options: Deregulation that let S&Ls make risky investments while deposits stayed insured

details.summary: The 1980s savings and loan crisis saw over 1,000 institutions fail after deregulation allowed them to make risky investments. Widespread fraud by executives who looted their own institutions cost taxpayers $132 billion.
details.whyItMatters: The S&L crisis demonstrated how deregulation without adequate oversight invites fraud. The $132 billion taxpayer bailout was the largest at the time and foreshadowed the 2008 crisis.
takeaways: Over 1,000 savings institutions failed in the 1980s and early 1990s
Executives used depositor funds for lavish lifestyles and bad investments
The taxpayer bailout cost $132 billion in 1990s dollars

faq.question: How did deregulation cause the S&L crisis?
faq.answer: Congress allowed savings institutions to invest in risky commercial real estate and junk bonds while keeping government deposit insurance. Owners gambled with depositor money knowing taxpayers would cover losses.

faq.question: Were S&L executives punished?
faq.answer: Unlike the 2008 crisis, over 1,000 S&L executives were convicted of criminal fraud. Charles Keating received a 12-year prison sentence. The aggressive prosecution stands in contrast to the lack of 2008 convictions.
